# Open findings register

Things measured, recorded, and **not fixed** — with no line item in any stage
of [NSOT_PLAN.md](NSOT_PLAN.md).

**Why this file exists.** Each of these was written into `CLAUDE.md` or a
stage document at the moment it was found, in prose, beside the thing it was
found next to. That is the right place to explain *why* something is true and
the wrong place to keep a list: prose accumulates invisibly, and the only way
to know what is outstanding was to have been present when each one was
recorded. The register is the list; the prose stays where it is and is linked.

**Rules.** An item leaves this file by being fixed, by being scheduled into a
stage, or by being closed with a reason. **A row that is fixed moves to
Closed in the same turn** (2026-09-28: 31 of 92 rows in the open sections
were done and had never moved, so the open count read about twice the work;
`tests/test_register_hygiene.py` now refuses a done row in an open
section). **A live exposure is listed here even when a stage owns it**: a
row with a home stopped counting as a finding, and NSOT_PLAN 6.1 sat outside
the triage built to catch it (C143). It does not leave by being
forgotten.

**The open count is a claim about DEFERRED work** (the operator, 2026-09-28). A row a stage owns lives in *Scheduled out of the register*, naming the stage, and leaves the open count; the stage's plan lists it. The open sections hold only what waits: A, B, UNKNOWN, and C deferred to Stage 9. Twice the register misled us about its own size (31 done rows never moved; then 26 of 61 open rows that were stage work), and both times the fix was a rule a test enforces: `test_register_hygiene.py` refuses an open row whose bucket places it in a stage other than Stage 9.

**The stopping rule for a sweep** (the operator, 2026-09-28, applied by default). A sweep may REGISTER whatever it finds, and only A items it finds are fixed in the same pass. Everything else waits, however cheap and however near the code being edited. A items found by fixing A items had begun to feed themselves (C155, C157, C158, C160), and "we are already in the file" is how a fix grows a second fix nobody triaged. C161 is the rule's first application: found inside C160's fix, in the same function, and left. Anything recorded as *"not applied"*, *"noted, not yet
addressed"*, *"recorded as a gap"* or *"left open"* belongs here on the same
day it is written.

**A register is only current if the reader checks the head.** A stale read
of a maintained file cannot be told apart from a stale file. On 2026-09-25 this
register was read at `1b9b4d3` while the repository was four commits ahead,
and three items already closed were raised again as open. That is the failure
this file exists to prevent, arriving through the reader rather than the
document. Before acting on an item, run `git log -1 -- docs/OPEN_FINDINGS.md`
and compare it with the head you are reading.

Status: **open** unless stated. Last reviewed 2026-10-07 (the charter triage below).

## Triage, 2026-09-28: every open row placed

**The rule (the operator's): a finding's SEVERITY is a claim about the world,
and claims about the world are measured, not assumed.** The findings that
turned out to be live exposure all read as tidying until something was
measured: C95 (masking, and it was a secret in a shared system), C141 (a code
default, and it was a published value) and C136 (cosmetic, and the import
could not be performed for 9 hours). The inverse held too (C135, C138, C142
real and harmless). So the classification depends on facts, and a row whose
severity rests on an unmeasured one is UNKNOWN until it is measured.

**The buckets, each a stated criterion:**
- **A, LIVE EXPOSURE**: true in the world now, and time makes it worse: a
  secret readable, a device unmanageable, data being lost.
- **B, BLOCKING**: something specific cannot be built or run until it is
  fixed. The row names what. If nothing is blocked, it is not B.
- **UNKNOWN**: could be A, and the fact that decides it has not been
  measured. Named with the one measurement and its cost.
- **C, EVERYTHING ELSE**: real, correctly recorded, and the tool works
  without it.

**Before sorting:** 92 rows sat in the open sections. **31 were already done**
and moved to Closed: 29 on their own row's evidence (FIXED, DONE or closed in
the status cell, never moved), and 2 measured done on the host tonight (C17's
URLs are set; E4's drift checker is enabled and ran at 05:47Z). C141 was
merged into C39, and C143 was added. **61 open.**

**The operator's question: was the triage a one-time sort, or do new rows
default to C? It was a one-time sort.** The re-triage's split (functional,
lab, minor) answers WHERE work goes, and it silently replaced the severity
axis (A, B, UNKNOWN, C) for every row recorded after it: C144, C145, C147 and
C148 each got a home and no bucket. By the criterion, **C148 is B (it blocks
the onboard-to-deploy loop, the product's central one)**, and **C147 was A
when it was recorded** (latent: the next device arriving with an RW community
would have had it written into the first permanent record; fixed the same
turn).

**Now structural:** every row in a live section, "Scheduled" included, opens
its status cell with ONE bucket, `**[A|B|UNKNOWN|C …; sorted <date>]**`. B
names what it blocks and whether that is on the critical path; UNKNOWN names
the measurement that would settle it; C names its kind (F functional, L
deferred for the lab, M minor) and its home.
`tests/test_register_hygiene.py` refuses a row without one, with a control.
**A new finding gets its bucket the turn it is recorded, with the criterion
applied, never assumed.**

| B9 | **CONFIRMED 2026-09-26: the off-box B2 key can destroy the backups it writes, without `deleteFiles`.** Run by the operator: `rclone delete -vv --include b2probe.txt` printed `Deleted` with no refusal, the normal listing was empty, and `--b2-versions` held the hidden version. `writeFiles` allows a HIDE, and the lifecycle deletes hidden versions a day later, so a compromised NMAS erases every off-box copy within 24 h. The first test (a single-file path: exit 0, file still listed) passed while proving nothing, because rclone's single-file check needs `readFiles`, so the file was never touched. **Fix: B2 Object Lock, Governance mode, default retention 16 days: the lifecycle's hide-after (15) plus its hide-to-delete (1)**, so no hide can delete anything sooner than the lifecycle would have. (First recorded as 15, which was a day short; corrected 2026-09-26) (docs/NETBOX_BACKUP.md §4). The semantics are from B2's documentation as understood here, and a five-step probe plan measures them before real data depends on them. **Closes when** step 4 of that plan shows a hidden LOCKED version surviving the lifecycle, and step 5 shows a governance bypass works. | **[C, L (Object Lock enabled, by the operator's account; not re-measured here); sorted 2026-09-28]** operator's step (measure, then enable) | docs/NETBOX_BACKUP.md §4 |
| B10 | **Nothing checks that the bucket's lock retention covers its lifecycle window.** **Decided 2026-09-26 (operator): a read-only key**, scoped to the bucket, which is ALSO the retrieval key (docs/NETBOX_BACKUP.md §6): one key, on the laptop to fetch and on the NMAS to check. It may live on the NMAS because everything it can read, the NMAS already holds unencrypted. Whether it can read the Object Lock retention is unknown until the check is built against the real response. It cannot write, so it cannot undermine what it checks, and a compromised NMAS can use it only to look. A manual check in the B2 UI was rejected: it is done once and never again, and this pair is exactly what drifts when one is changed and the other forgotten. **The property to check is not "both are 15"** but **lock retention >= daysFromUploadingToHiding + daysFromHidingToDeleting**. Shorter fails, because files become deletable before the lifecycle removes them: the hole re-opening silently. Longer warns, because the lock has silently become the retention. | C1427 | **Verify keys an adjacency by its neighbour, so a second adjacency to the same neighbour has no check of its own** (the operator, Lab 8 step 4, 2026-10-20): r4 and r3 are adjacent twice, over Gi3 (the shared segment) and Gi4 (the /31), and the plan's "What verify checks" named one adjacency to 10.255.1.13. CORE. | **[C, re-sorted 2026-10-20 ~09:0x UTC from B, measured in the code: Verify DOES fail a lost parallel adjacency. `pipeline`'s neighbour read counts the table's ROWS (`len(rows)`, one per adjacency: r4 reads 6 with both r3 rows), and any drop past the expected ones fails after the settle window, so losing either r3 adjacency fails Verify. What remains: (1) "What verify checks" draws one row per neighbour, fewer than Verify judges (a display that understates); (2) a program that drops BOTH parallel links on purpose subtracts the expected drop once and fails Verify, rolling back a correct change (none in Labs 8 or 9). Neither touches R6's single adjacency to R4, so it does not block step 6 (the overnight run's reading; the operator had asked for it before R6's deploys on the premise above)]** The original reading, for the record: `expected_effects.expected_ids` and `neighbour_ids` are sets of router-ids, and `offers()` de-duplicates ends by protocol and router-id without the interface, so two adjacencies give one row; the pipeline subtracts the count of unique router-ids from a per-row count (`pipeline.py` around 1463), so a program that shuts both links to one neighbour expects one drop and sees two (a false failure), and Verify judges each protocol by its count, not row by row. An interface joined by `ip ospf N area A` alone is not an expected adjacency (`neighbours.ospf_links` reads network statements only). The fix: an adjacency keyed by (protocol, neighbour, interface), one check each, judged per row, with a test on r4's two-interface table. | `modules/nsot/verify_scope.py` |

| C695 | **r4 drops traffic for r3's ISP peering address while advertising a default into OSPF** (found 2026-10-12 by C693's measurement, through Mercury's reads engine; the register searched first). r1, r2 and s4 split traffic for 198.51.100.1 over their OSPF default's two next hops, r3 and r4; r4's own `show ip cef 198.51.100.1` is "0.0.0.0/0 no route", and r3's for 198.51.100.3 (r4's peering) the same: each edge router originates a default "always" without holding one, and neither carries the other's peering /31. So a flow hashed to the wrong edge router for the other's peering address is dropped. Judged LAB against the charter: the lab network's routing design, not Mercury's; the trace reports it correctly. **Measured 2026-10-12 03:22 to 03:27 UTC (the operator's list), read-only through Mercury's reads engine on r3 and r4 only, each read recorded:** (1) **neither edge holds a real default**: `show ip route 0.0.0.0` is "% Network not in table" on both, and both carry `default-information originate always` under `router ospf 1` and `ipv6 router ospf 1` (OSPFv3 also `redistribute static`). (2) **r5 advertises three prefixes to each edge**, the same to both: 8.8.8.8/32, 10.255.1.15/32 (r5's loopback) and 203.0.113.0/31; each edge holds all three from its own eBGP session (no iBGP between r3 and r4; nothing redistributed between BGP and OSPF). Each edge advertises 0 IPv4 prefixes to r5 (`prefix-list NO-PRIVATE out`, no `network` under IPv4). (3) **Nothing r5 advertises is blackholed**: Path… from r1 and r2 to 8.8.8.8, 203.0.113.1 and 10.255.1.15 splits over r3 and r4, and both hand it to r5; r1 pings 8.8.8.8 5/5 from its loopback and from Gi2, and r3 and r4 each 5/5 (so r5 routes the fleet's addresses back by means Mercury cannot read). (4) **Only the two peering /31s are affected**: r1 pings 198.51.100.1 0/5 (its flow hashes to r4) and 198.51.100.3 5/5. An address r5 does not advertise (192.0.2.1) is dropped at whichever edge: there is no real default anywhere, while the fleet's OSPF says there is. **Read again 2026-10-22 ~03:2x UTC from Lab 8's VLAN 10** (read-only through Mercury, r7 sourcing from Gi3.10): R5's r4-facing addresses answer 5/5 in both families (198.51.100.3; 2001:DB8:51:1::2, traced r7 → r6 → r4 → r5), its r3-facing ones do not (198.51.100.1 `U.U.U`; 2001:DB8:51::2 `XXXXX`). In IPv6 the drop has its own mechanism: r4 has no route for r3's peering /64, so 2001:DB8:51::2 matches r4's own `ipv6 route 2001:DB8::/32 Null0` (the static behind its BGP `network 2001:DB8::/32`) and is discarded there; option (a)'s OSPFv3 half removes it. **The fix options, each the operator's pick (no device change made):** (a) **the peering /31s into OSPF, passive** (`network 198.51.100.0 0.0.0.1 area 0` and `passive-interface GigabitEthernet2` on r3; `198.51.100.2 0.0.0.1` on r4; the OSPFv3 equivalent for the IPv6 peerings): every router learns each /31 at the edge that holds it, so that address goes only there; no adjacency with r5; fixes exactly this symptom and changes nothing else. (b) **a conditional default** (`default-information originate always route-map <map>`, the map matching a prefix learned from r5): an edge whose eBGP session is down stops attracting traffic; failover, not the /31s. (c) **iBGP r3–r4 with next-hop-self** (update-source Loopback0, over OSPF): each edge also learns r5's routes through the other, so a flow sent to an edge whose own session is down still leaves; the /31s only if each edge also advertises its connected /31 into BGP (`network 198.51.100.0 mask 255.255.255.254`). (a) is the smallest that fixes C695; (b) or (c) adds failover. Each is a deploy through Mercury (intent, preview, verify), the BGP or OSPF settle windows applying. | **[C, lab design; sorted 2026-10-12]** measured; the fix is the operator's pick of (a), (b), (c) or a combination. | the lab's r3 and r4 configuration |

The second purpose is why attribution stays strict where the security argument alone might have relaxed it, and any change to the role model is checked against both. | **[C, L; sorted 2026-09-28]** build | [NSOT_AUTHORIZATION.md](NSOT_AUTHORIZATION.md); NSOT_PLAN.md *AUTHZ* |

The per-lab backup runs as `cp -r … 2>/dev/null; rsync …`. The `;` means a failed backup does not stop the overwrite it exists to protect. Whether a destination can commit (repo present, git identity) is found only after every file is written. The run then ends with "Startup-configs updated." as its LAST line, after the failure block. The fix has three parts. Check every destination's preconditions before copying any. Gate each rsync on its backup (`&&`). | C272 | **Every command re-sent on a session still carrying the first one's output, and verify passed or failed on what it could not read** (found with C271, 2026-10-01; the operator: "a verify that can't read reliably must say so, not pass or fail on stitched text"). `run_device_command` probed a `show` for 10 s, then re-sent it with `send_command_timing` on the SAME session, and verify's own reads (`show ip ospf`, `show ip bgp`, `show interfaces`) were in that short-probe list, read right after a push and a save, when the deploy's session read its prompt as `^@`. A show reply holding an echoed command or the session's own prompt raises `UnreliableRead`. A read that raises SPENDS its session (`config_read.SPENT_ATTR`): nothing reads it again, and the connection pool replaces it, so a later read gets a new session. The pipeline's reads ask the pool at each read (`_conn_of`), so one bad read leaves the rest of a snapshot readable. Before the push, a snapshot read that cannot be trusted refuses the deploy with nothing sent, naming the command and why. After it, the post snapshot and the canary read on a NEW session (the push's is closed), a routing read that failed goes to the settle window to be read again on a new session, and what still cannot be trusted (a protocol, routes, interfaces, the config the removals are checked against, BGP at its hold time) is `unreadable`: verify does not pass, does not fail on it, rolls nothing back for it, and the receipt, the result ("could not be read reliably after the change ... capture the device to read it again") and Needs attention say so. The alert rules use the same query, so a broken applet's own error read as a sign of life: the unsafe direction. | C20 | A settings-route test failed intermittently, echoing `kea_username` as `''`. | 2026-09-25 | **Two causes, both measured and fixed, neither the one first suspected.** **(1) The test failure: import-time binding.** `modules.integrations.base` binds `get_setting` by name. When `test_onboard_plan.py` ran before anything imported `app`, `base` was first imported inside that file's `lab` fixture, while `settings_schema.get_setting` was a lambda answering unlisted keys with the schema default. `base` kept the lambda. An import hook recorded the import, on the main thread, with the lambda bound. The order was deterministic: 3 of 3 failed with that file first, 2 of 2 passed with it second. The **streaks were my subset command**: `grep` in the tool shell is a parallel `ugrep` and returns files in varying order. `conftest.py` now imports `app` before any test runs, as the program does, and a subprocess test runs the failing order. **(2) Found while chasing it, and worse: concurrent settings writes CORRUPTED the file.** A probe recorded every write during a failing run and saw only the route's own two, both correct, so the redaction refresh and the background threads were ruled out by measurement. But `save_user_settings` used one temp name for every writer, and no read-modify-write held a lock. Two threads × 150 writes left `user_settings.json` unreadable in 2 of 2 runs, and the unreadable-file guard then refused every write. Fixed: a per-write `mkstemp`, and `config.settings_lock()` (an RLock, plus `flock` across processes) around all four read-modify-write sites. After the fix: 300 of 300 keys, threads and processes, 3 of 3 runs. An AST scan requires the lock in any function that both loads and saves. The general-settings POST was one of the four, and it **bypasses `write_settings()`**, so CLAUDE.md's *one write path* was not true. |
